56.0.s.en: (1) The deliverance of those who trust in God

56.0.0.en: 1- “Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up; he fighting daily oppresseth me.” 2- “Mine enemies would daily swallow me up: for they be many that fight against me with pride.”

56.0.1.en: Would swallow me up: is about to devour me.

56.0.2.en: 1- David takes refuge in God and complains to Him about Saul and those with him, who pursue him and are hostile to him though he is innocent, and try to fight him and destroy him, and keep on pursuing him all the day, that is, all the time, because Saul kept pursuing David for many years until the end of Saul’s life. David’s taking refuge in God declares his faith in God’s power, which is able to protect him, and that however strong man is, he is weak before God, and however much this man feels his pride and strength, he is nothing before the greatness of God.

56.0.3.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about the enemies of the people of God in every generation, such as Sennacherib in the days of King Hezekiah, Nebuchadnezzar in the days of King Zedekiah, and King Antiochus in the days of the Maccabees; indeed, it is a prophecy about the Jews who opposed Christ, and in general about the devil and the demons who fight men throughout time. All of these are marked by pride, cruelty, a tendency to shed blood, continual fighting, and seeking to destroy the innocent.

56.1.0.en: 3- “What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.”

56.1.1.en: When David went to Gath to hide from the face of Saul, he feared that the Philistines would discover that he was David, who had killed Goliath years before, but he trusted in God, who is able to protect him even in the midst of enemies. Here two things appear:

56.1.2.en: a- David’s courage in confessing his fear.

56.1.3.en: b- David’s faith in God and his trust in Him, and not in any other power in the world.

56.2.0.en: 4- “In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.”

56.2.1.en: Since David trusted in God, who is able to do all things, he no longer feared earthly, limited men, but on the contrary believed God’s promises and trusted them, that God is able to protect him, and he boasted, that is, he praised, thanked and glorified God, because He is his great God, able to do all things.

56.3.0.en: 5- “Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil.”

56.3.1.en: 1- David’s enemies tried to twist his words, that is, to interpret his words with other meanings he did not intend, and to catch some wrong word against him. Their hearts were evil toward him, so they watched him and tried to accuse him with false accusations all day long, that is, they kept on presenting him in a bad light, and stirred Saul up against him (1 Sam 24:9), and Saul himself stirred up the Jews against David in order to be rid of him.

56.3.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, against whom the Jews, throughout His ministry to them, tried to catch some wrong word, and accused Him with many false accusations.

56.4.0.en: 6- “They gather themselves together, they hide themselves, they mark my steps, when they wait for my soul.”

56.4.1.en: 1- David’s enemies were not content with twisting his words, but resolved to destroy him, and so they did the following:

56.4.2.en: a- “They gather themselves together”: so that their number would be large and it would be easy for them to seize him.

56.4.3.en: b- “They hide themselves”: to surprise him when he is unprepared and destroy him.

56.4.4.en: c- “They mark my steps”: they watched David’s movements through spies.

56.4.5.en: d- “They wait for my soul”: they prepared to destroy me.

56.4.6.en: 2- All this too is a prophecy about Christ and what the Jews did to Him.

56.5.0.en: 7- “Recompense them for their iniquity. In anger bring down the peoples, O God.”

56.5.1.en: In the spirit of prophecy David saw what would befall the wicked, namely that God will punish them for their iniquities and show the wrath of God the Judge upon them, so that they are brought low under the strong hand of God in eternal torment. God may also punish them in their life on earth, that they may perhaps repent and return to Him. The Philistines attacked Saul many times, killed many and seized some of the cities of the children of Israel, that perhaps Saul would take notice and repent, but he did not repent, and died in the war.

56.6.0.en: 8- “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?”

56.6.1.en: Thy bottle: the bottle is a vessel made of skin, also called a waterskin, in which wine was kept in ancient times, or in which water was carried.

56.6.3.en: 1- Though the enemies watched David to catch him by a word or to destroy him, at the same time David was confident that God watches his movements and his flight from place to place from the face of Saul, in which he appears as one wandering, that is, that the eye of God watches him, tends him and protects him, and therefore his enemies cannot harm him.

56.6.4.en: 2- In the midst of the many tribulations David passed through, he lifted up his prayers to God and his tears flowed; he even wept for the wicked who did not repent, and wept at the loss of his loved ones, and even of those who were hostile to him, namely Jonathan, Saul, Abner and Absalom, and he also wrote a lament for them (2 Sam 1:23; 2 Sam 3:33, 34; 2 Sam 18:33). And he wept most of all over his sins (Ps 51). All these tears carried and expressed strong feelings from the depths of David, so he asked God to accept them, keep them with Him and care for them.

56.6.5.en: 3- Though people do not care about his tears, and may despise him because of them, or at least may make light of them, he is confident that God does not neglect them. So he asks Him to keep his tears in a bottle with Him, that is, every tear has great value with God, because God says to every soul in the Song of Songs, “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me” (Song 6:5). Tears draw out God’s mercies and stir His tenderness, and He even writes their memorial in a special book with Him, to reward David, and everyone who weeps before God, with great blessings on earth and in heaven. This, of course, is different from the tears of people shed over the loss of material things or worldly attachments they were attached to; these tears are not for God’s sake, and God does not keep them with Him, because they take people away from God.

56.6.6.en: 4- The Jews kept wine in a bottle, and wine signifies joy, so this indicates that God rejoices in the tears of His children poured out before Him, and gives them peace and joy on earth, and then joys in heaven that cannot be expressed.

56.6.7.en: Be confident that God cares about all your prayers and your crying to Him, and regards your tears with great regard, because your feelings are precious to Him when you direct them to Him. So do not listen to the doubts of Satan, who tells you that God has forgotten you, for He gathers your prayers and your tears and rewards you for them at the time that is right for you.

56.7.0.en: 9- “When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back: this I know; for God is for me.” When David noticed that God takes care of him and tends him, his heart was assured that God is for him and not for his enemies, and that He will protect him and keep the evils of his enemies away from him. If they try to attack him they will be defeated and turned back, since God’s power defends him. What matters is that David keep praying and calling upon God, and so be assured of God’s protection and care for him.

56.8.0.en: 10- “In God will I praise his word: in the LORD will I praise his word.” 11- “In God have I put my trust: I will not be afraid what man can do unto me.”

56.8.1.en: These two verses repeat (v. 4) in this psalm; it is like a refrain repeated in this psalm, or this spiritual hymn, to confirm the purpose of the psalm, which is the praise of God, on whom His children trust, and so enjoy blessings beyond counting. The two verses were explained before at (v. 4).

56.9.0.en: 12- “Thy vows are upon me, O God: I will render thank offerings unto thee.”

56.9.1.en: David believed that God would save him from his tribulations and bring him back to Jerusalem, and even crown him king, because He had anointed him by the hand of Samuel, and would save him from his enemies, so he made promises of the following:

56.9.2.en: a- Fulfilling the vows to God, which it seems he had made while fleeing from the face of Saul.

56.9.3.en: b- Offering thank offerings to God, which are peace offerings, as the Law of Moses prescribed. David fulfilled this when he brought back the ark of the covenant of God and offered sacrifices in abundance (2 Sam 6:13) and was in great joy.

56.10.0.en: 13- “For thou hast delivered my soul from death: yea, my feet from slipping, that I may walk before God in the light of the living.”

56.10.1.en: a- Because God delivered him from certain death to which he was exposed many times.

56.10.2.en: b- God also delivered him from slipping into wrong conduct or corrupt opinions that take him away from God and deprive him of the Kingdom, especially since his tribulations were severe, and he even lived among the pagans for a time, fleeing from Saul.

56.10.3.en: c- Walking in the way of light, that is, holiness, and carrying out God’s commandments: this is the light of the living with God, whose end is the perfect light of the living for ever in the Kingdom, where there is full enjoyment of the light of God. The light of the living is also the light of the living saints in heaven, whose way of life we imitate and who help us by their prayers.

56.10.4.en: God wants you to live in the light of the living all your days, so look to Him, for He is the true light, and make friends with His saints, for they are the first to be enlightened by Him; then you will be able to remain steadfast in His Church, enjoy her sacraments, and love prayer and meditation, so that you live enlightened and are alive before Him for ever. Thanksgiving to God my Savior. To the chief Musician, Al-taschith (Destroy not), a golden psalm (Michtam) of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave: “Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me” (v. 1) Introduction:

56.10.6.en: 2- When was it written? When David was fleeing from the face of Saul and hid in a cave in the wilderness of En-gedi (1 Sam 24), and while he was hiding Saul entered and slept at the mouth of the cave, but David did not kill him; he cut off the skirt of his robe, and thanked God, who had rescued him from Saul’s hand, and even delivered Saul into his hands, and then David forgave him.

56.10.7.en: 3- This psalm suits every person who passes through many tribulations and is surrounded by his enemies, and lifts his heart to God his Savior, and after He rescues him thanks God and praises Him.

56.10.8.en: 4- The words of this psalm were set to a tune called “Destroy Not,” and the two psalms following this one, (Ps 58, 59) and also (Ps 75), were set to the same tune. The words “Destroy not” may refer to a musical instrument with nine strings that accompanied the presentation of the psalm.

56.10.9.en: 5- This psalm is considered one of the distinguished psalms that David composed; therefore it is called a golden psalm (Michtam), and the Jews used to write it in gold ink.

56.10.10.en: 6- This psalm was sung by a group of Levites led by a leader called the chief Musician. So it is a liturgical psalm sung by the congregation of the children of Israel gathered in the house of God, especially in times of tribulation and pain.

56.10.11.en: 7- This psalm is counted among the Messianic psalms, because it tells us of many events in the life of Christ, such as Christ’s resurrection early at dawn on Sunday (v. 8), and it tells us of His ascension to heaven (v. 5).

56.10.12.en: 8- The last part of this psalm (vv. 7-11) is repeated in (Ps 108:1-5).

56.10.13.en: 9- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Sixth Hour, in which Christ was crucified; therefore it tells us of the tribulations that Christ met, but after He died He rose from the dead.

57.0.0.en: 1- “Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast.”

57.0.1.en: 1- David asks God for mercy twice, because of his great need of His help and protection. Asking for mercy twice indicates the need of the Jews and the Gentiles for mercy.

57.0.2.en: 2- David asks for God’s protection under His wings, and God likened Himself to a hen gathering her chicks under her wings (Lk 13:34). God’s protection is complete and protects from all calamities and problems. The wings of God may signify His incarnation in the fullness of time. The two wings are marked by the ability to protect and to snatch away quickly one who needs protection, that is, they indicate the speed of God’s answer to those who seek Him.

57.1.0.en: 2- “I will cry unto God most high, unto God who defends me.”

57.1.1.en: 1- Because of David’s great need of God to save him from Saul’s pursuit, he cried out to Him, and this cry also confirms his faith in God, who is able to protect him.

57.1.2.en: 2- In the spirit of prophecy David cries out to Christ the Savior, crucified at the Sixth Hour, to save him with the rest of mankind who believe in Him. Indeed, Christ who cries out while on the Cross proclaims the need of mankind to cry out to God to save it.

57.2.0.en: 3- “He shall send from heaven, and save me, he reproacheth him that would swallow me up. Selah. God shall send forth his mercy and his truth.”

57.2.1.en: 1- Saul pursued David and tried to kill him, but God kept David, and on the contrary made Saul fall under David’s hand, and then David’s virtue appeared, which is forgiveness. Here the God who saves appears, who sent and arranged from heaven David’s salvation, and reproached and showed the weakness of Saul, fallen at David’s feet. So the one who wanted to devour David was turned into a weak person fallen at David’s feet. Thus appeared God’s mercy, which rescued David, and His truth and justice, which made Saul fall weak at David’s feet.

57.2.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about the incarnate Christ, whom the Father sent to save mankind, and who reproached the devil and even bound him by the Cross, and mercy and truth were fulfilled in the person of Christ, who redeemed mankind and condemned Satan by His Cross.

57.2.3.en: 3- The word Selah is in this verse, after the reproaching of the enemy and the proclamation of salvation from heaven, so that in this musical pause man may contemplate the power of God, who saves His children from the hand of the demons and the wicked.

57.3.0.en: 4- “My soul is among young lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.”

57.3.1.en: Set on fire: the wicked, inflamed with the fire of evil.

57.3.2.en: Spears: the plural of spearhead, which is the weapon of the lance, that is, its pointed end.

57.3.3.en: 1- David likens Saul and his company who pursue him to young lions, whose teeth are like the points of spears and arrows, and whose tongues are like swords, to show the fierceness of his enemies, their violence and their plots. But all this did not make David troubled; he slept among his enemies, who were set on fire with the fire of evil, in security, because God protects him, so that no one can come near him, and on the contrary he made his enemy Saul fall at his feet in the cave.

57.3.4.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about the plots of the Jews, which ended in the crucifixion of Christ, but He slept at rest on His Cross at the Sixth Hour, and then rose to offer redemption to mankind.

57.4.0.en: 5- “Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth.”

57.4.1.en: 1- David asks God to be exalted above the heavens, that is, to show His glory above all the angels, and while He shows His greatness above the heavens, He lifts up David and all who love God to enjoy fellowship with Him. His glory is also exalted over the earth, that is, God’s glory appears above all the glories of men and their works, which are great in their own sight, and the weakness of men appears and their evils become nothing before His glory and power.

57.4.2.en: 2- David speaks in the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who is exalted above the heavens and over the earth, for after hiding His divinity by His incarnation He rises from the dead and then ascends to heaven, that is, is lifted above the earth in great glory until He is hidden among the clouds, to draw the hearts of His children to heaven, so that they pray at all times.

57.5.0.en: 6- “They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down: they have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves. Selah.”

57.5.1.en: 1- While David’s heart is attached to the great, glorified God, as appeared in the previous verse, the other side appears, which is the wicked’s dealing with him, and it appears in the following:

57.5.2.en: a- The snares that the wicked prepared for him during their pursuit of him for many years.

57.5.3.en: b- The threats and the continual attempts to destroy him had a very strong effect on him, so that he expressed it by saying that his soul was bowed down under these pressures.

57.5.4.en: All this shows the violence of the enemies and the extent of the pain David suffered.

57.5.5.en: 2- The snares that Saul set for David to seize him turned into a snare for Saul himself, for while Saul was pursuing David, he entered and rested in the cave where David was staying, and so the enemy pursuer, Saul, became an easy prey, and David came forward to cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe, and he could have destroyed him, but he forgave him. So Saul fell into the pit he had dug for David, and the pursuer became prey, while the pursued, David, became a mighty man by the power of God.

57.5.6.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, for whom the Jews set many snares, and bowed His soul with grief throughout His ministry on earth, and in the end dug a pit for Him, the Cross, and destroyed Him, and His power appeared; for by His death He bound Satan, because He paid the debt for mankind who believe in Him, and so He made Satan fall into the pit, and Satan could not bind Christ, but he himself was bound, and after the Cross he can no longer cast the children of God into Hades.

57.5.7.en: 4- At the end of this verse we find the word Selah, a musical pause in which the psalmist contemplates the power of God, who changes situations and rescues His children until He saves them from all their enemies.

57.5.8.en: Look to Christ your Savior and your stronghold and contemplate His beauty, and He will captivate your mind, gladden your heart and give you peace, and the plots of the demons or all the tribulations that pass over you will no longer disturb you, because your heart is occupied with God. Thus you will be lifted up to heaven while you are on earth.

57.6.0.en: 7- “My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise.”

57.6.1.en: 1- When David’s heart was attached to God, who is exalted above the heavens, his heart was assured and became steadfast in God, not troubled by the enemy’s threats or the changes of life, and this steadfastness became a motive for his quiet spiritual growth, so that he enjoyed fellowship with God.

57.6.2.en: 2- The continued steadfastness of David’s heart moved him to praise God; because David is settled, his eyes were enlightened and he saw God clearly, and so he sang and chanted to Him, and then God revealed His glory to him, and he shared with the heavenly ones in their praise.

57.7.0.en: 8- “Awake up, my glory; awake, rebab and oud: I myself will awake early.”

57.7.1.en: Early: the early morning is the end of the night, just before dawn.

57.7.2.en: Rebab: musical instruments each of which has a single string.

57.7.3.en: Oud: a stringed musical instrument still known today.

57.7.4.en: 1- David believed that God would rescue him from his enemies because he had seen God’s works with him; though he was still pursued by Saul, God had rescued him several times, so his heart was assured, and he felt that his glory is God. In his solitude he called his glory, God, to awake within him, and felt the strength within him, and praised God with the rebab and the oud; indeed, his heart was so attached to God that he awoke at the early morning to praise God before dawn.

57.7.5.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about the resurrection of Christ, to whom “my glory” refers, so we praise Him with musical instruments, and even awake at the early morning to praise Him, because our hearts have been attached to Him.

57.7.6.en: 3- This verse is also a prophecy about the Holy Spirit, to whom the word “my glory” refers, so we praise Him with power and at all times.

57.7.7.en: 4- The early morning refers to the whole of life that we live on earth, in which we ought to awake to praise God, before the dawn of our life rises, which is eternal life.

57.7.8.en: 5- The Talmud mentions that when David went to sleep he would hang an oud above his bed, and in the middle of the night, when the north winds blew, they would move the strings of the oud, which produced beautiful melodies that woke him from his sleep to read in the Law of God, and then praise and glorify His holy name until the early morning.

57.8.0.en: 9- “I will praise thee, O Lord, among the people: I will sing unto thee among the nations.”

57.8.1.en: 1- David cannot do without God, so even if he fled to the Philistines from the face of Saul he keeps on praying, chanting and thanking God, because God is his life.

57.8.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about the acceptance of the Gentiles into faith in Christ, so that they chant David’s psalms, believe in Christ and praise Him.

57.9.0.en: 10- “For thy mercy is great unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds.”

57.9.2.en: 1- David felt that God’s mercy had covered those who believe in Him, and forgave them their very many sins, and lifted these weak ones to heaven in their conduct, purity and exalted life, and the glories of heaven await them.

57.9.3.en: 2- God’s truth, which is His justice, shines forth to the clouds, that is, the heavens, where the righteous are glorified with God, while the wicked are cast into torment.

57.10.0.en: 11- “Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: let thy glory be above all the earth.” Here David repeats the verse found in (v. 5), to confirm his longing that God be glorified, and that this glory appear in the heavens and on the earth. And mankind enjoys the glory of salvation in Christ Jesus, as we explained before at (v. 5).

57.10.1.en: How beautiful it is to awake early to pray and begin your day with speaking to God. Take care to pray before any other work. Ask your guardian angel to wake you early, and know that God your Father is waiting to hear your prayer and rejoices in it.

57.10.2.en: God the just Judge. To the chief Musician, Al-taschith (Destroy not), of David. A golden psalm (Michtam): “Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation?”… (v. 1) Introduction:

57.10.3.en: 1- Its writer: David the prophet, as mentioned in the title.

57.10.5.en: When David was exposed to flight from the face of Absalom and saw evil coming upon him, he asks God, the just Judge, to rescue him and save him.

57.10.6.en: 3- This psalm is sung to the tune “Destroy Not,” and “Destroy not” may be a musical instrument that accompanies the psalm, as we mentioned in the previous psalm.

57.10.7.en: 4- The subject of this psalm is the attack on unjust judges and rulers, that perhaps they will repent, and reminding them of the destruction that awaits them, while on the contrary blessing and joy await the righteous.

57.10.8.en: 5- This psalm is one of the distinguished psalms and so is called a “golden psalm (Michtam),” and it may have been written in gold ink.

57.10.9.en: 6- This psalm is sung by a group of singers who have a leader, or director; therefore it is written in the title “to the chief Musician.”

57.10.10.en: 7- This psalm is considered one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the wicked Jews rising up against Christ and crucifying Him, but He rejoiced that He had accomplished the salvation of mankind.

57.10.11.en: 8- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
